newsitem.title: KENYA: Experts meet on U.N. environment agency, reforms.
newsitem.headline: Experts meet on U.N. environment agency, reforms.

text.p: Experts from 100 nations and agencies met in Nairobi on Monday with the rich countries seeking cuts and reforms in the U.N. environment agency and the poor seeking more aid for the global environment.
They met after the head of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP), Elizabeth Dowdeswell, lamented budget cuts caused by key donors failing to pay their dues while demanding reforms in the U.N. system.
Dowdeswell was opening a two-week meeting of UNEP's Governing Council, its top legislative and policy organ.
Western governments are critical of the U.N. agency, saying it appeared less effective since the 1992 Earth summit in Brazil.
The Earth summit, the U.N. Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), gathered world leaders in Rio de Janiero, where they made fresh commitments to environmental protection.
"This is likely to emerge as UNEP's most highly politicised council meeting," a delegate in Nairobi told Reuters.
"It looks like the environment will take second place at this meeting in preference to issues of reform and financial accountability," a Western diplomat said.
Western governments led by the United States want UNEP, the only global U.N. agency based in the developing world, to refocus on its core tasks.
These are identified as monitoring the state of the planet, identifying emerging issues and initiating global responses to them and promoting the development of international law.
The United States has spearheaded calls for steep cuts in the UNEP budget as part of its attack on U.N. agencies it considers wasteful, inefficient or outdated.

But Third World nations disagree and want powerful, wealthy nations to raise funding for UNEP so it can effectively concentrate on managing and using natural resources, and building a better environment for human health and well-being.

"The issue at hand is whether UNEP is financially strong enough to carry out its core tasks. Frankly it is not in a position to do so because of a weak financial base caused by the West," an African ambassador told Reuters.
Dowdeswell told a plenary session earlier on Monday budget cuts were undermining UNEP's ability to manage the environment.
"Member states have reduced their overall contributions to UNEP, while at the same time imposing ever-increasing responsibilities on UNEP," she said.
The governing council meets every two years at UNEP's Nairobi headquarters and is normally used to approve a programme on managing natural resources and improving the environment.
But this year's forum is being sidetracked by talk of reforms and financial woes because of the reluctance of some Western donors to pay their dues.
Dowdeswell said 18 of UNEP's 58 member countries, including three major donors, reduced contributions last year while only 37 percent of member states contributed to its Environment Fund.

Key donors such as Japan, United States, Britain, France and Italy are reluctant to pay. UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link more funding to reforms in the agency.
From a budget of $160 million during UNEP's 1991-92 programme, UNEP's budget provision fell to $105 million in the last two years and even then only $62.5 million was disbursed by donors.
UNEP is preparing a budget of up to $80 million for the next two years but many experts doubt the powerful West will pay.
New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised to reform the entire U.N. system and has made reform a constant theme since his election last December.
Washington vetoed his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, charging him with failure to press reform of the 185-nation organisation with sufficient vigour.
